claims.text: Periodic interfaces in HEA multilayer coatings act as barriers to stress-assisted dislocation climb.
Periodic interfaces in HEA multilayer coatings impede diffusion.
Multilayer interfaces promote local solute segregation and mechanical mismatch.
Interface-mediated obstruction of climb and diffusion significantly reduces creep relative to homogeneous HEA coatings.
The proposed multilayer coating has alternating microstructural or compositional characteristics and nano- or microcrystalline layers.
Diffusion-assisted creep processes can be active in HEAs at intermediate to high temperatures under sustained load.
Local variations in phase, composition, and lattice parameter at multilayer interfaces create dislocation-pinning points.
Solute enrichment at multilayer interfaces locally slows lattice diffusion.
Creep in HEAs under high temperature and load is generally governed by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion.
Layer boundaries interrupt dislocation motion and reduce effective diffusion paths.
Layer boundaries increase the energy barrier for dislocation climb.

Under identical temperature and loading conditions, multilayer HEA coatings will have a significantly lower creep strain rate or accumulated deformation than homogeneous coatings of the same composition and thickness.
TEM examination after creep will show reduced dislocation activity at multilayer interfaces.
Microstructural examination will show limited diffusion phenomena at multilayer interfaces.
The proposed interface mechanism applies only in temperature and stress ranges where diffusion-assisted creep dominates.
At extremely high temperatures or loads beyond material stability limits, beneficial interface effects may diminish or coating failure may occur.
The magnitude of creep-rate reduction may depend on processing parameters.
